title: The Pame Game
bodyHtml:
The languages Northern and Central Pame belong to the Oto-Pamean branch of the Oto-Manguean language family. They are spoken in separate states of Mexico by approximately 5620 and 4350 people, respectively. Like all languages belonging to the same family, they have preserved some features of the proto-language (the common ancestor language of the family) but have changed in other features, making the languages similar yet different from one another. These differences can be in both the structure of the grammar and in the pronunciation of words. To help you know how words in these languages are pronounced, the following key is given to the pronunciation of the symbols:

tvoiceless alveolar plosive (the first sound in English tea)
dvoiced alveolar plosive (the first sound in English do)
nvoiced alveolar nasal (the first sound in English new)
svoiceless alveolar fricative (the first sound in English see)
rvoiced alveolar flap (the sound made by the r in the Spanish word pero)
lvoiced alveolar lateral (the first sound in English lead)
tʃʼvoiceless alveolo-palatal ejective affricate (similar to the first sound in English chew)
ɲvoiced alveolo-palatal nasal (similar to the ny sound in canyon)
kvoiceless velar plosive (the first sound in English key)
gvoiced velar plosive (the first sound in English goo)
kʼvoiceless velar ejective (similar to the first sound in English key)
ʔvoiceless glottal plosive (the sound between the vowels in English uh-oh)
hvoiceless glottal fricative (the first sound in English he)
alow unrounded vowel (similar to the sound in English ah)
emid front unrounded vowel (similar to the sound in English eh)
ihigh front unrounded vowel (the first sound in English eat)
omid back rounded vowel (similar to the sound in English oh)
uhigh back rounded vowel (the first sound in English oops)
ḭhigh front unrounded vowel produced with glottal fry
ũhigh back rounded vowel with nasal airflow

Some numbers from Northern Pame are given below:

9 = kara tenhiuɲ sante
13 = kara tenhiuɲ gitʃʼaḭ
17 = kanuje tenhiuɲ sante
20 = kanuje tenhiuɲ giriuḭ
26 = karnuʔ tenhiuɲ nuji
30 = karnuʔ tenhiuɲ tiria
35 = giriuḭ tenhiuɲ rnuʔ

Here are some arithmetic equalities in Central Pame (note that × means multiplication):

(1)nda ntsawʔ + seskaʔai nda ntsawʔ nda = nda lien tiliɲũhũɲ
(2)kiɲui + nda ntsawʔ = seskaʔai nui
(3)nda lien nda × nui = nui lien nui
(4)tiliɲũhũɲ + kikʼai = tilija × nui
(5)seskaʔai ranhũʔ × ranhũʔ = nda lien seskaʔai nda ntsawʔ nda
(6)seskaʔai kikʼai + kikʼai = nui × seskaʔai
(7)kikʼai + ranhũʔ = nda ntsawʔ
(8)nda + nui = ranhũʔ

Answer the following questions in the Answer Sheets:

B1. Given that the following equality is satisfied:

Northern PameCentral Pame
(9)teriuhiɲ × kara tenhiuɲ nuji= ranhũʔ lien seskaʔai

a. Convert the following Northern Pame numbers to numerals:

  • nuji
  • karnuʔ tenhiuɲ teriuhiɲ

b. Write out the following numbers in Central Pame:

  • 1
  • 3
  • 9
  • 56
  • 60

hints.text: Start with Northern Pame. One word, tenhiuɲ, shows up in every single number given. Line up the numerals (9, 13, 17, 20, 26, 30, 35) with the words around that repeated word and ask what arithmetic operation the repeated word could stand for.

Northern Pame counts in groups of eight: a number looks like multiplier, then the base word, then an addend. Watch out - the smallest numbers have one word when they act as a multiplier and a different word when they act as an addend. Central Pame instead counts in twenties with a ten as a stepping stone, and one word means "times twenty". Because the two languages are related, cognate (shared-ancestor) words help you match them, and equality (9) gives you the same quantity written in both languages, which pins down the last Northern Pame value.

Worked example (not a graded answer): 9 = kara tenhiuɲ sante and 13 = kara tenhiuɲ gitʃʼaḭ. Both start with kara tenhiuɲ, and 13 - 9 = 4, so the difference is entirely in the last word. If kara tenhiuɲ is one group of eight plus something, then sante contributes 1 (8 + 1 = 9) and gitʃʼaḭ contributes 5 (8 + 5 = 13). Use the same subtraction trick on the other Northern Pame pairs, then move on to Central Pame.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: find the shape of a Northern Pame number

Every Northern Pame number in the list contains the word tenhiuɲ, with one word before it and one word after it. That is a strong clue that a number is built as multiplier - base - addend: something times a fixed base, plus something extra.

Compare two numbers that share their first two words:

  • 9 = kara tenhiuɲ sante
  • 13 = kara tenhiuɲ gitʃʼaḭ

The only difference is the last word, and the numerals differ by 4. So the last word is the addend. Now compare 9 with 17 = kanuje tenhiuɲ sante: the last word is the same, and the numerals differ by 8. So changing the first word from kara to kanuje adds exactly 8. The base is 8, and the pattern is

(multiplier) tenhiuɲ (addend) = 8 x multiplier + addend.

Step 2: read off the Northern Pame digits

With base 8, take each line apart:

  • 9 = 8x1 + 1, so kara = 1 (multiplier) and sante = 1 (addend).
  • 13 = 8x1 + 5, so gitʃʼaḭ = 5.
  • 17 = 8x2 + 1, so kanuje = 2 (multiplier).
  • 20 = 8x2 + 4, so giriuḭ = 4.
  • 26 = 8x3 + 2, so karnuʔ = 3 (multiplier) and the addend for 2 is nuji.
  • 30 = 8x3 + 6, so tiria = 6.
  • 35 = 8x4 + 3, so giriuḭ = 4 again as a multiplier, and the addend for 3 is rnuʔ.

Notice something odd: 1, 2 and 3 each have two words - one used as a multiplier (kara, kanuje, karnuʔ) and one used as an addend (sante, nuji, rnuʔ). From 4 upward there is only one word (giriuḭ is used in both slots). That answers the first item of part a immediately.

Only one addend slot is still empty: 7. It must be teriuhiɲ, the one leftover word that appears in equality (9) - and equality (9) confirms it, as we check below.

Step 3: crack Central Pame with algebra

Now treat each Central Pame word as an unknown and solve the equalities like puzzles, starting with the shortest:

  • (8) nda + nui = ranhũʔ and (7) kikʼai + ranhũʔ = nda ntsawʔ. The smallest whole numbers that fit a chain like this are 1 + 2 = 3 and 5 + 3 = 8.
  • Check with (6): seskaʔai kikʼai + kikʼai = nui × seskaʔai. If seskaʔai = 10, then seskaʔai kikʼai = 10 + 5 = 15, and 15 + 5 = 20 = 2 x 10. It works, so seskaʔai = 10 and putting a word after seskaʔai means "ten plus that".
  • (4) tiliɲũhũɲ + kikʼai = tilija × nui: 7 + 5 = 6 x 2, so tiliɲũhũɲ = 7 and tilija = 6.
  • (2) kiɲui + nda ntsawʔ = seskaʔai nui: something + 8 = 12, so kiɲui = 4.

That leaves lien and the longer strings. In (3) nda lien nda × nui = nui lien nui: if lien means "times twenty, plus", then this reads (1x20 + 1) x 2 = 2x20 + 2, i.e. 21 x 2 = 42. Correct. Check (1): 8 + (10 + 9) = 27 = 1x20 + 7, which matches nda lien tiliɲũhũɲ. And (5): (10 + 3) x 3 = 39 = 20 + 19, which matches nda lien seskaʔai nda ntsawʔ nda. So Central Pame is base 20 with 10 as a helper, and 9 is expressed as nda ntsawʔ nda, literally 8 + 1.

Step 4: the bridge between the two languages

Equality (9) says a Northern Pame product equals a Central Pame number. On the Central side, ranhũʔ lien seskaʔai = 3x20 + 10 = 70. On the Northern side, kara tenhiuɲ nuji = 8x1 + 2 = 10, so the multiplier teriuhiɲ must be 70 / 10 = 7 - exactly the gap we spotted in the Northern Pame table. Now karnuʔ tenhiuɲ teriuhiɲ = 8x3 + 7 = 31.

Step 5: building the requested Central Pame numbers

  • 1 = nda, 3 = ranhũʔ - straight from the list.
  • 9 = 8 + 1 = nda ntsawʔ nda.
  • 56 = 2x20 + 16, and 16 = 10 + 6, so 56 = nui lien seskaʔai tilija.
  • 60 = 3x20 exactly, with no addend, so it is simply ranhũʔ lien.

The two related languages kept a similar shape for numerals (multiplier, base word, addend) but chose different bases - eight in the north, twenty with a ten in the centre - a nice illustration of how sister languages drift apart while keeping family resemblances.
_reviewNotes: Answer keys are taken from the official solution page. Please verify two transcription choices against the PDF glyphs: (1) the vowel glossed "high front unrounded vowel produced with glottal fry" is transcribed here as i with COMBINING TILDE BELOW (ḭ), appearing in gitʃʼaḭ / giriuḭ - confirm the booklet does not use a different subscript diacritic (e.g. combining minus/plus below); (2) glottal stop is transcribed as IPA ʔ (booklet prints it as a question-mark-like glyph), e.g. karnuʔ, ntsawʔ, seskaʔai, ranhũʔ - accepted variants allow typing "?" instead. The multiplication sign in the Central Pame equalities is transcribed as U+00D7 (×); the booklet prints a heavy saltire-style multiplication cross - check font coverage. No figures require cropping.
